title: Short Stuff: Khipu
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss whether the Inca Empire had a written language. They cover the Inca's scale (roads of roughly 25,000 miles, a large population across the Andes) and their administration of tribute. The main subject is the khipu, a cord device of knotted strings. Leland Locke in the 1920s argued khipus recorded information, and they were used for numerical record keeping such as censuses and tribute. Gary Urton, a Harvard anthropologist, later argued from the 1990s onward that khipus also encode names and abstract ideas. His student Manny Madrono reportedly extended the decoding, and Scottish researcher analysis of colonial-era khipus found narrative-like symbols. The hosts conclude a written language likely existed but remains undeciphered, and that much of it was lost when khipus were destroyed by the Spanish.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about dad jokes and puns, then introduce the topic of whether the Inca had a written language.

segments.title: Inca Empire overview
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Inca Empire's size, including roughly 25,000 miles of roads through the Andes and millions of people. They explain the tribute system between clans, villages, and Inca rulers, and note they built a large empire without an apparent written language.

segments.title: What the khipu is and early views
segments.summary: The khipu is described as a cord of knotted strings, often cotton or llama or alpaca wool, hung from a thicker cord. Early observers thought it was art or crafts, and many were destroyed by the Spanish.

segments.title: Leland Locke and khipu as record keeping
segments.summary: In the 1920s Leland Locke, studying khipus at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, argued they encode information. The hosts say they were used for numerical record keeping, such as tribute and censuses, working like an abacus.

segments.title: How khipu knots encode numbers
segments.summary: Knot position, type, color, material, direction, and loop count all carry meaning. Knots in decimal positions represent place value, so the knots' arrangement encodes numbers.

segments.title: Gary Urton, Manny Madrono, and evidence of language
segments.summary: Gary Urton, a Harvard anthropologist, argued from the 1990s that khipus include names and abstract ideas. His student Manny Madrono reportedly extended the decoding. Evidence includes khipus found in burials and a St. Andrews University researcher's analysis of colonial-era khipus that describe a war. The hosts conclude the Inca likely had a written language that is still undeciphered, and that it was lost much as if English monks had died out.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and point listeners to the web and email.
